prime.problem: A team adds tracing and thinks it has evals, or collects thumbs-downs and thinks the agent is learning. Then the same failure ships again after the next model or prompt change, because nothing that saw it could stop a release.
prime.fits: First card of the evidence course. The claim chain showed that 'done' needs evidence per link; this card asks who keeps that evidence, who judges it, and how a judged failure changes what ships next.
expect: feedback vs learning, and the release gate
answer-changing artifacts ("a change in the ruler")
prime.goal: Name which of the four jobs a given record or signal does, say what would have to exist for a failure to become impossible to re-ship, and design a gate that a rising average can't fool.

attend: Why should a trace and an audit record share a run ID but live in different stores?
The Tuesday run's trace records exit 1 perfectly. Why does that not make it an eval?
In the loop diagram, why is the dashboard drawn off the loop while the release gate is on it?
Why does changing a grader count as shipping something, even though the agent didn't change?
How can the overall pass rate go up while a release should still be blocked?

must: A trace records what happened, not whether it was acceptable → a perfect trace can document a bad run → judgment needs a separate eval that asserts the path and the final state (the checker's exit 1, approval-before-refund)

A side effect needs accountability, not just debugging → trace and audit share IDs but not storage → merging them makes the debug stream too sensitive to share and the audit record too weak to answer 'who authorized this'

A signal (thumbs-down, bad trace, failed eval) changes nothing by itself → an owner labels the root cause and writes a regression case → a release gate runs it and blocks the release if the failure returns → only then has the system 'learned'

Anything that can change an answer (model, prompt, tool description, context, index, metric, policy, grader) → is a deployable → needs a version, an owner and a test, and a grader change needs a frozen human-labelled set so a 'change in the ruler' isn't read as an agent improvement
elevated: Overall pass rate is a case-weighted mean of slice rates → a 20% slice can fall from 90% to 50% while the overall rises 82% → 86% → gates need per-slice floors and hard blockers (policy failures, known regressions)

Message contents are opt-in in the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and flagged as likely PII → traces are a sensitive data store → they need retention, access control, redaction and sampling, and the run record should point to sensitive data rather than copy it
reference: OTel GenAI operation names: invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool, retrieval (status: Development; repo semantic-conventions-genai)
content attributes gen_ai.input.messages / gen_ai.output.messages are opt-in; gen_ai.usage.input_tokens / output_tokens are recommended
OpenAI Evals API: read-only 31 Oct 2026, shutdown 30 Nov 2026
Part 7's release path: change manifest → component evals → end-to-end suite → repeated trials → slice comparison → review → shadow or canary → rollout → monitoring → promote or roll back
replay levels in Part 7: exact, behavioural, diagnostic reconstruction

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the evidence loop from memory (run → … → what ships) and mark where audit, the dashboard and incoming signals attach. Then write 3–4 sentences on why a thumbs-down is not learning.
checklist: trace = what happened; audit = under what authority; eval = was it acceptable; feedback = a signal
audit hangs off the trace by a shared run ID, only needed for side effects
the dashboard informs but stops nothing; the release gate is the box that changes what ships
signals → triage with an owner → regression case → gate
every answer-changing artifact, graders included, is versioned, owned and tested
gates read slices and hard blockers, not one average

retrieve.q: Your team says "we have full observability, every model call and tool call is traced, so we know the agent is good." Explain what that claim confuses, using the Tuesday run.
answer: a trace answers 'what happened', not 'was it acceptable'
the Tuesday trace records pytest exit 1 at step 6 and the false 'Done' at step 9 faithfully
deciding it failed needs an eval: the checker's re-run, an assertion on final state

retrieve.q: A support agent issues a wrong refund at 3 AM. Walk the failure through the loop until it can no longer ship again. Name each artifact it becomes.
answer: the trace reconstructs the path; the audit record shows which identity authorized which account and amount
triage labels the root cause and assigns an owner
the case becomes a dataset item and a regression test
the release gate runs it and blocks any release where it fails again

retrieve.q: You swap your LLM judge for a newer model and the eval score jumps 6 points with no agent change. What do you do before believing it, and why?
answer: a grader is an answer-changing artifact: version it like a deployable
score both judges against a frozen human-labelled set
if agreement shifted, the ruler moved, not the agent

retrieve.q: Why keep trace and audit records separate when they describe the same run, and what does it cost you?
answer: different jobs: diagnosis vs accountability
merged, the debug stream is too sensitive for broad access and the audit record too weak
cost: two stores, and you must keep shared IDs so they can be joined

compare.q: The claim chain checks one run link by link; the evidence loop runs across many runs and releases. What does each one decide, which one could have stopped the Tuesday run's false claim, and which stops it from happening again next month?
answer: the claim chain decides whether this run's 'done' is true (effect verified fails)
an eval on that run catches it; the claim chain is in effect the eval's checklist
only the loop, through a regression case and a release gate, stops the same failure from re-shipping

compare.q: Measuring an agent compares two harness versions on a fixed task set. What does the evidence loop add on top, and how does each fail when used alone?
answer: the loop adds where cases come from (production failures), who owns them, and a gate that blocks releases
evals alone: a fixed set ages as production moves and misses the cases you didn't know to write
the loop alone without honest eval statistics: a gate reacting to noise, or one average hiding a broken slice

compare.q: The forensics method checks an agent's claims against the evidence its runs leave behind, with negative controls. How is that the same job as a trace plus an eval, and what does the loop do with a finding that a one-off experiment doesn't?
answer: both set a claim against recorded evidence: what happened vs what was said
forensics is a deliberate experiment pinned to one release; the loop runs on every production run and release
the loop turns a confirmed failure into an owned regression case and a gate, so the finding keeps protecting later releases

predict.q: A team's eval set is built entirely from past production incidents, and every release must pass all of them. After a year the gate never fails, yet users keep reporting new problems. Before reading on: what has gone wrong, and which control from the card would have shown it?
predict.answer: The offline set only protects known failures; production keeps creating cases nobody wrote down, and the question distribution drifts. Part 7 says offline gates aren't enough: you also need sampled production review, canaries, shadow runs and online monitoring split by signal (satisfaction, reliability, correctness, governance, drift), feeding new cases back in. A gate that never fails is protecting yesterday's workload.

apply.task: Run python3 code/evidence-loop.py. Then change the candidate's finance slice to 33/40, 34/40 and 36/40 in turn, and before each run predict SHIP or BLOCK. Finally keep finance at 36/40 and set the Tuesday regression to False.
apply.done: You get: 33/40 → overall 185/200 = 92%, BLOCK ('finance: 82% < floor 85%', 'finance: down 8 points'); 34/40 → 186/200 = 93%, SHIP; 36/40 → 188/200 = 94%, SHIP; Tuesday regression failing → 94%, BLOCK ('known regression back'). And you can explain why 34/40 ships although it sits exactly on both limits (85% floor, 5-point drop).
apply.hint: The script compares exact fractions. Print 0.9 - 0.85 in Python to see what a float gate would have done at 34/40: the drop comes out a hair above 0.05 and blocks. 'At the limit' needs a deliberate rule, and someone who owns it.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 34/40 gate result, or the never-failing gate?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why trace and audit are separate, or why a grader change is a release?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: signal → owned regression case, or regression case → release gate?
In your own agent, which answer-changing artifact has no version or owner today?
What would your first per-slice floor be, and who would own it?
